edge_kinds.code_refs: source files this document names by path — what it claims about
edge_kinds.code_refs_missing: paths it names that DO NOT EXIST; each is a defect
edge_kinds.referenced_by_code: source files whose comments send a reader here

claim_kinds.fenced_blocks: total fenced blocks; each is a claim about something
claim_kinds.rust_blocks: blocks purporting to be this project's Rust — must match the source
claim_kinds.output_blocks: blocks purporting to be terminal output — must match a real run
claim_kinds.identifiers: backticked Rust items that must still exist
claim_kinds.external_terms: claims about kernel/POSIX/format behaviour needing a citable source

excluded.target: build output; contains vendored dependency docs, not ours
excluded..agents/DOC-REVIEW.md: this scanner's own output. Without this the map is not idempotent: run one writes the checklist, run two finds it and adds it as a node.

order_strategy: what must be understood first, in five tiers: the project's own account of itself, then the phase docs in pipeline order, then the threading deep-dives, then process and release records, then templates. Deliberately NOT link depth: these documents barely link to each other while depending heavily on shared context, so link depth would order them almost arbitrarily.
review_focus: Verify each document against the code it describes. This session's code review already found four kinds of drift — a quoted bar template with the wrong spacing, quoted ioctl snippets that no longer matched, a paraphrase of --help presented as output, and a phrase naming a dependency the library no longer has — so quoted code, quoted output, named identifiers and named paths are the four things to check first.

files.verdict: sound after one fix; the densest technical claims in it all held

findings.kind: claim invalidated by the code review, and its reasoning undercut
findings.what: the identity re-check was described as three fields — rdev, model, size — with the note that 'the model and size comparisons back up the rdev check'
findings.why: DeviceIdentity carries five; serial and wwid arrived during identity.rs's review. Worse than a short list: the sentence names model and size as the backstop, and those are precisely the two that cannot see the likely accident, since two sticks of the same make and capacity are equal in all three of rdev, model and size. The document explained the mechanism and then named the wrong guard for it.
findings.disposition: fixed: all five named, with why the three were insufficient and which VPD page each new field comes from

findings.kind: message described as saying more than it does
findings.what: 'EBUSY ... The error message points to that directly' — that being udisks2 racing in
findings.why: the message reads '(EBUSY => someone else holds the device)'. It does not name udisks2, and a reader expecting it to would think they had a different fault.
findings.disposition: fixed: quotes what the message says and keeps the udisks2 diagnosis as the doc's own

findings.kind: the O_EXCL semantics, tested rather than read
findings.what: all three conditions in the claim list, and both manual-test claims
findings.why: swap active on a loop device makes O_EXCL fail with EBUSY and swapoff clears it; a plain O_RDWR holder does not conflict, exactly as the manual test says; a second O_EXCL holder does, with errno 16; and bd_prepare_to_claim is real, at block/bdev.c:573. This file's O_EXCL description is also the correct one — it does not carry the false partition claim that phase_2.rs's own module doc had, which I corrected during the code review.
findings.disposition: no action

findings.kind: a limit the documentation implied but never stated
findings.what: the identity section explained why serial and wwid were added without saying how often they are actually available
findings.why: a maintainer ran .agents/verify-on-hardware.sh against a SanDisk 3.2Gen1: model present, serial and wwid both absent. So on that stick the two new fields compare None to None, pass, and the check falls back to rdev+model+size — the exact combination the section says cannot separate two identical sticks. The strengthening is inert on a very common brand, which makes the fallback the normal path rather than an edge case.
findings.disposition: fixed: recorded as a field report, with the point that this is the device's limit rather than the check's, and that a stick exposing page 0x83 gets a strictly stronger guarantee than one that does not

findings.what: the field report said serial and wwid were both 'absent'; they fail differently
findings.why: a second hardware run showed serial has no file at all, while wwid has a file that returns ENXIO — SCSI registers the attribute for every device and the read fails when there is no VPD page 0x83 behind it. imi maps both to None correctly, but testing Path::exists before reading would conclude this stick has a WWID when it does not.
findings.disposition: fixed in the doc, and pinned by a new test in sysfs.rs that simulates a failed read with a directory where the file belongs. Verified it bites by writing the exists-then-read shape into device_attr_in.

findings.what: 'The kernel's do_fcntl whitelist for F_SETFL accepts: O_APPEND, O_NONBLOCK, O_NDELAY, O_DIRECT, O_NOATIME, O_ASYNC'
findings.why: SETFL_MASK in fs/fcntl.c is exactly the first five. O_ASYNC is settable but by a different route — setfl calls the file operation's ->fasync() handler, which owns the FASYNC bit, and only for file types that implement it. Presenting six flags as one mask hides that a future contributor relying on O_ASYNC's presence in the mask would be reasoning about a mechanism that does not exist.
findings.disposition: fixed: the mask quoted verbatim with its application line, and O_ASYNC's separate path described
